It didn?t worry me much until I started discharging huge blood clots  as big as an apple 2 times every after 30 mins from that moment.   I rushed to the ER later that night(still bleeding heavily with blood clots every now and then) but I was not admitted since my vitals and the blood counts were normal at that moment.   I went back home  and hoped the bleeding would stop but again with on pain or fever what so ever I kept bleeding all day. This is my 5th day of bleeding. However, the cause of the bleeding still remains unknown.

Chief complaint: Syncope.   The patient was seen on paramedic arrival to room #2 with the above chief complaint.  She is a very pleasant otherwise healthy 38-year-old woman who had been in her usual state of health.  Today she felt a little lightheaded, laid down on the floor in her kitchen, and had a syncopal spell.  This occurred roughly an hour prior to arrival and lasted just a few minutes.  When her mother arrived she stated that she had witnessed the spell and that the patient was tonic but not having seizure-like activity.  She was completely unresponsive and confused afterwards but not incontinent.  She is describing nausea but no chest discomfort.  She has had no vomiting or diarrhea and no diaphoresis.  She denies prior similar symptoms and has no history of seizure, heart disease, VTE, or reactive airway disease.  She does feel like she has a dry mouth and also feels improved at this time.  She is not on medications chronically.  She did have her second COVID-19 vaccination yesterday with some mild arthralgias but nothing else.  She was seen by the paramedics and noted to be having dropped beats.  An EKG was obtained and during transport she went into a complete heart block with resumption of sinus rhythm afterwards.  The EMS rhythm strip was reviewed by myself and does reveal transient complete heart block.       DETAILS OF HOSPITAL STAY   Hospital Course Summary Patient is an 38 y.o. female w/ no significant PMHx who presented to the ED via EMS after a syncopal episode.  She was standing in the kitchen, felt lightheaded then fell to the floor and passed out.  Her mother subsequently arrived and witnessed an additional episode of of unresponsiveness.  EMS subsequently caught on telemetry multiple episodes of complete heart block.  The longest of these lasted 20 seconds.  She was referred for admission.  The interested reader is referred to the complete admission history and physical.   Patient is admitted to the hospital.  Pacer pads were placed.  On monitor she had no further symptoms nor pauses.  Cardiology consulted.  Echocardiogram was performed and was normal.  It was ultimately felt that the patient most likely experienced a vagal event with marked suppression of AV conduction.  Of note, patient received her second Pfizer COVID-19 vaccination the day prior.  Cardiology has recommended discharge home with a Zio patch.  Lengthy discussion has been held with patient regarding importance of immediately activating EMS should she have recurrent symptoms similar to what brought her in.   Patient was also noted to have a microcytic anemia.  Iron studies returned remarkable for severe iron deficiency.  She received 1 dose of IV iron in the hospital and is discharged with twice daily oral iron.  She is to follow-up with her PCP for ongoing monitoring and evaluation.  In addition, she should lay down immediately.

The case is of TEN (toxic epidermal necrolysis) and concurrent COVID-19-associated hyperinflammatory syndrome (cHIS) successfully treated with systemic corticosteroids and etanercept. The patient with a history of ascending aortic dissection status post aortic root and aortic valve replacement on warfarin presented with a 2-day history of painful rash. His only new medication was trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 160-800 mg twice daily, started 4 days prior to rash onset and discontinued the following day. Two days preceding the rash, he developed a fever to 38 Celsius degree. Review of systems was negative for cough, sore throat, rhinorrhea, or congestion. He was vaccinated and boosted with the BNT162b2 (Pfizer-BioNTech) vaccine. Nasopharyngeal polymerase chain reaction test for SARS-CoV-2 was negative. On admission, his vital signs were unremarkable. His dermatologic examination demonstrated bilaterally injected sclera with yellow-white crusting around the eyelid margins and a 3-cm erosion on the hard palate. Painful red macules coalescing into patches covered 90% of his body surface area, with extensive flaccid bullae creating a "cigarette paper" appearance. Nikolsky sign was positive. Laboratory testing was notable for serum bicarbonate of 19 mmol/L (normal 20-30 mmol/L). Skin biopsy of the right upper back demonstrated an acute basket-woven stratum corneum, widespread, confluent keratinocyte necrosis with focal adnexal involvement, and modest inflammation. The diagnosis based on clinicopathological correlation was TEN, with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole as the suspected drug culprit. He was initially treated with a single dose of methylprednisolone 125 mg IV (2 mg/kg prednisone equivalent) and etanercept 50 mg subcutaneously. On day 2, he became febrile with a temperature of 39.3 Celsius degree. On day 4, he tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 by nasopharyngeal polymerase chain reaction. Laboratory testing was notable for C-reactive protein of 276.5 mg/L (normal 10 mg/L) and ferritin of 1465 ng/mL (normal 30-400 ng/mL). On day 5, he began a 5-day course of dexamethasone 6 mg and received a second etanercept dose. On day 6, he received tocilizumab 8 mg/kg IV and began a 5-day course of remdesivir 100 mg. On day 7, he required intubation and mechanical ventilation due to agitated delirium requiring sedation. While intubated, he required low positive end-expiratory pressures and a low fraction of inspired oxygen. Initial reepithelization was observed on day 7. His hospital course was complicated by Pseudomonas bacteremia and Clostridioides difficile colitis, for which he received IV piperacillin-tazobactam and PO vancomycin, respectively. Complete reepithelization was observed by day 15. He was extubated on day 17 and discharged home on day 23. This case report describes the first successful treatment of TEN and concurrent cHIS with systemic corticosteroids and etanercept in the literature. His SCORTEN (Score of Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis) was 3 and the ABCD-10 severity-of-illness score (age, bicarbonate, cancer, dialysis, 10% body surface area) was 2. Follow-up information has been requested.; Sender's Comments: Based on the information given in narrative, the causal relationship between the event and the suspect drug BNT162B2 cannot be excluded.

symptom_text: On 12/23/2021, I received my Pfizer booster. Almost 24 hours later on 12/24/2021, I started having persistent cardiac arrhythmias. I felt nauseous and fatigued. I checked my O2 saturation, which was normal. However, my blood pressure was high and my heart rate fast. I wasn't able to do anything without feeling faint. At about 4 PM, I blacked out while walking through my house and fell. My adult son came over to have Christmas dinner, and he expressed concern, because I didn't look well. I would move from one room to another and immediately have to sit down, because I would get dizzy. My blood pressure was up, and I kept checking it; it was 170/120 with no exertion. My elevated blood pressure and dizziness lasted for about 10 days. The blood pressured dropped to about 140/95 after about 5 days. I was hesitant to call my doctor, because I was sure I would be told to go to the ER. I was terrified to go to the ER, because I knew they were swamped, plus I was afraid I would contract COVID. Instead, I ate healthy food, drank plenty of water, and I got up to walk through the house about once every hour. I slowly got better, but at the time of this writing, I still have occasional episodes of rapid heart rate without exertion and a feeling of faintness. Whenever I climb the stairs, my heart intermittently starts pounding; this never happened until I got the booster.

symptom_text: Almost immediately after the vaccine on  1/23/2021, the patient started having what she described as little "flutters" on her L side (patient states she usually she gets them in her chest) this time on the  left side, almost like a "strike" = per patient like a painful electric shock down her side. Worsened and on 1/9/2022 taken to the ED. Exam there showed tenderness at mid sternum. XR was normal and an EKG was normal. In the ED, the patient reported the episodes stopped. Thought likely some component of costochondritis. Told to f/u with cardiology.   Seen by Cardiology;  on exam had reproduced left lower sternal border pain with palpation, no murmurs. EKG normal.  CXR was clear. Tested for COVID twice and negative, also flu negative.  Then after about a week she felt better and was cleared for physical activity. However, on 1/29/2022  during the second half of a field hockey game she began to "not play right", walking rather than running, experiencing vague dizziness and chest discomfort, and feeling as though her heart was beating kind of funny.  Over the next 20 minutes, these symptoms progressed. When she was taken out of the game to rest, she walked over to the shade because she was feeling weak and "really hot".  She was "not walking right", fell to the ground, but did not experience actual LOC, bodily injury, tongue biting or urinary incontinence.  She was picked up and placed on the nearby training table, where she remained awake but showed some delay in responding to questions.  Her mother noticed that she had perioral pallor at that time.  She was ultimately put in to an ambulance, and taken to the ED, where extensive testing was performed: negative thyroid function screen, D-dimer, sed rate, CRP, BNP, procalcitonin, CBC, BMP, total CK, and viral tests (Covid, flu, RSV). In addition, she had a negative chest x-ray and normal echocardiogram.  Initial serum troponin I was 0.09 ng/mL (upper limit of normal in that facility was 0.05 ng/mL) - trending showed drop in troponin to 0.03 and then <0.03 by the next morning.  She was observed in the ICU, and had a benign exam and ECG tracings.  It was recommended that she follow-up with cardiology after discharge. Afterwards she still continues to have symptoms of "fluttering" in her chest (longstanding), but to date no other symptoms.  A followup troponin and CRP on 2/14/2022 were normal.  Cardiology thoughts: Numerous published reports re: mild transient serum troponin elevation in exercising individuals, seems to reflect normal physiological response rather than pathological process. Considering evaluation for rare congenital coronary artery anomalies with chest CT angio.

COVID vaccine (single dose of Pfizer vaccine)-induced ITP/refractory ITP; This is a literature report for the following literature source(s).  Introduction: Vaccine-induced de novo cases of immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) after COVID-19 vaccination have been described in the literature, with severity thought to be directly correlated with vaccine potency in inducing an immunologic response in the patient. Most cases, however, were found to be benign and responsive to typical immunosuppressive therapies1. Here describe a case of refractory ITP first induced by the COVID-19 vaccine, as well as subsequent development of biopsy-proven secondary Hemophagocytic Lymphohistiocytosis (HLH). Case: 71-year-old female with a complex history of COVID vaccine (single dose of Pfizer vaccine)- induced ITP diagnosed in March 2021. In prior admissions, she was treated with steroids, romiplostim, vincristine and IVIG, and eventually started on rituximab. Her current admission was for syncope secondary to warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia with admission hemoglobin level of 4.7. Hemolysis was confirmed by reduced haptoglobin, indirect hyperbilirubinemia, anemia and negative cold agglutinins, positive DAT IgG antibodies. Initial treatment included IVIG, alternate day plasmapheresis and high dose steroids. Extensive infectious, autoimmune and malignancy work up was done and found to be negative. Slow improvement in hemoglobin was noted, but the case was complicated by severe refractory thrombocytopenia and hypofibrinogenemia. Hematology recommended a bone marrow biopsy, which demonstrated hemophagocytosis suggesting a diagnosis of secondary HLH thought to be secondary to an autoimmune process. Soluble CD25 (soluble IL-2 receptor alpha) was elevated and CXCL9 was negative. Currently, she is improving but remains inpatient, and is on mycophenolate with a slow steroid taper. Discussion and conclusion: This case illustrates an example of refractory ITP that is non-responsive to multiple lines of therapy with treatment ongoing as of this writing. Furthermore, the patient's course is complicated by warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia and biopsy-proven HLH secondary to a likely autoimmune etiology.; Sender's Comments: Based on the temporal relationship, the association between the event refractory thrombocytopenia with BNT162b2 can not be fully excluded. symptom_text: After receiving second dose, patient experienced strong side effects, such as extreme fatigue, fever lasting a week, increased appetite, headache, and vertigo. The symptoms cleared up after a week, however several days later the patient began experiencing disequilibrium. It was a feeling of rocking/swaying back and forth even when standing still. Although the patient had previously occasionally experienced vertigo, they had never experienced disequilibrium prior to May 2021. The feeling came on suddenly and unexpectedly, with no identifiable trigger. On the first and second occasions it lasted only about an hour or so. Once the patient sat down for an extended time, the feeling went away. However, beginning on July 17, 2021 the patient again experienced extreme fatigue along with intense disequilibrium, to the point that the patient could not stand or walk without tipping over. The intense fatigue again lasted for a week and then cleared up, but the disequilibrium remained. At this point the patient sought medical care from their doctor. The doctor examined the patient's ears and indicated that the inner ear passage was experiencing inflammation from an unknown cause. The patient conducted a blood test, which came back normal, and was advised to take Flonase for two weeks. Patient began taking Flonase but had to stop after 5 days due to an adverse reaction (tongue swelling, brain fog, rapid heartbeat) from the Flonase. Patient was advised to try Claritin. They did so but stopped after a few days as the disequilibrium was not improving. The disequilibrium was continually present for two months, to varying degrees each day, and no treatment helped to alleviate symptoms. In mid-September the disequilibrium abated and was only present about 2-3 days a week. It continued to gradually lessen until October, where there was a two week period at the end of the month where no disequilibrium was experienced. Beginning on November 3, 2021 the patient again experienced unexplained extreme fatigue coupled with disequilibrium. The patient took a Covid PCR test which came back negative. The fatigue cleared up after one week but the disequilibrium remained. The patient continues to experience daily disequilibrium and has been tracking the intensity of symptoms since October 1, 2021. Symptoms seem to worsen (with the disequilibrium becoming especially intense) approximately one week before the patient begins menstruating, and then returns to less intense symptoms after about 3-5 days.

symptom_text: This is a literature report. The reporter reported two reports for same events for 2 patients, this is the first of the report. Recently reported cases of myocarditis and pericarditis after coronavirus disease 2019 (Covid-19) messenger RNA (mRNA) vaccination.1 In recently published reports, diagnosis of myocarditis was made with the use of noninvasive imaging and routine laboratory testing. Here, authors report two cases of histologically confirmed myocarditis after Covid-19 mRNA vaccination. Patient 1, a 45-year-old woman without a viral prodrome, presented with dyspnea and dizziness 10 days after BNT162b2 vaccination (first dose). A nasopharyngeal viral panel was negative for severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), influenza A and B, enteroviruses and adenovirus A serum polymerase-chain reaction (PCR) assay and serologic tests showed no evidence of active parvovirus, enterovirus, human immunodeficiency virus, or infection with SARS-CoV-2. At presentation, she had tachycardia ST-segment depression detected on electrocardiography which was most prominent in the lateral leads and a troponin I level of 6.14 ng per milliliter (reference range, 0 to 0.30). A transthoracic echocardiogram showed severe global left ventricular systolic dysfunction (ejection fraction, 15 to 20%) and normal left ventricular dimensions. Right heart catheterization revealed elevated right- and left-sided filling pressures and a cardiac index of 1.66 liters per minute per square meter of body-surface area as measured by the method. Coronary angiography revealed no obstructive coronary artery disease. An endomyocardial biopsy specimen showed an inflammatory infiltrate predominantly composed of T-cells and macrophages, admixed with eosinophils, B cells, and plasma cells received inotropic support, intravenous diuretics methylprednisolone (1 g daily for 3 days), and, eventually, guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure (lisinopril, spironolactone, and metoprolol succinate). Seven days after presentation, her ejection fraction was 60%, and she was discharged home. In these two adult cases of histologically confirmed, fulminant myocarditis that had developed within 2 weeks after Covid-19 vaccination, a direct causal relationship cannot be definitively established because we did not perform testing for viral genomes or autoantibodies in the tissue specimens. However, no other causes were identified by assay or serologic examination. No follow-up attempts are possible; information about lot/batch number cannot be obtained. No further information is expected. Sender's Comments: Based on temporal association and available information a contributory role of BNT162b2 to the reported fulminant myocarditis cannot be excluded.  Case will be reassessed if additional information is received. The impact of this report on the benefit/risk profile of the Pfizer product is evaluated as part of Pfizer procedures for safety evaluation, including the review and analysis of aggregate data for adverse events. Any safety concern identified as part of this review, as well as any appropriate action in response, will be promptly notified to regulatory authorities, Ethics Committees, and Investigators, as appropriate. acute kidney injury; minimal change disease presenting with nephrotic syndrome; minimal change disease presenting with nephrotic syndrome; This is a Literature report.  As mass vaccinations for coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) are being administered worldwide, rare reports of adverse events are emerging. We report a case of minimal change disease presenting with nephrotic syndrome 1 week after a first injection of the COVID-19 vaccine (Pfizer-BioNTech). A 77-year-old male with a 15-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus without retinopathy received a first dose of the Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine on March 17, 2021. Medical history included obesity, prior smoking, and coronary artery disease. Baseline serum creatinine ranged from1.0 to 1.3mg/dl, with no proteinuria over the previous year. Outpatient medications included atorvastatin, aspirin, dulaglutide, empagliflozin, glipizide, losartan, metformin, and metoprolol. There was no history of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug use. Seven days after vaccination, he presented to his local physician complaining of abrupt onset of lower-extremity edema. Laboratory testing revealed 4+proteinuria by dipstick and serum albumin of 2.5 g/ dl. Nephrology consultation 12 days after vaccination(29-MAR-2021) found anasarca with 13.6-kg weight gain due to edema, elevated blood pressure (152/81 mm Hg), and 4+ proteinuria on urinalysis with inactive urine sediment, prompting hospital admission. Laboratory evaluation by 14 days after vaccination(31-MAR-2021) showed 24- hour urine protein of 23.2 g/d, serum creatinine of 2.33 mg/ dl, and serum albumin of 3.0 g/dl. Complete blood cell count was normal, and hemoglobin A1c was 7.5%. Serologies included elevated C3 and C4 and negative hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis C antibody. A kidney biopsy was performed 16 days after vaccination (02-APR-2021). Among 7 glomeruli sampled for light microscopy, 4 were globally sclerotic and 3 were histologically unremarkable. There was 25% tubular atrophy and interstitial fibrosis with moderate arteriosclerosis. Cortical tubules displayed diffuse acute epithelial injury. No immune deposits were identified by immunofluorescence (2 glomeruli) or electron microscopy (2 glomeruli). Electron microscopy revealed 100% podocyte foot process effacement, leading to a diagnosis of minimal change disease with acute tubular injury. The ultrastructural findings of minimal segmental mesangial sclerosis and glomerular basement membrane thickening (mean, 460 nm) suggested underlying mild diabetic changes. Empiric pulse methylprednisolone, 1 g daily for 3 days, was initiated on hospital admission, followed by oral prednisone, 60 mg daily, after biopsy. In the hospital, he required i.v. furosemide drip, 10 mg/h, transitioned to bumetanide, 0.25 mg/h, for 5 days for fluid overload. Creatinine peaked during the hospitalization at 3.17 mg/dl at 19 days after vaccination(05-APR-2021). The patient was discharged 3 days later(08-APR-2021) with 19.8 g/g proteinuria by spot ratio, serum albumin of 2.9 g/dl, and serum creatinine of 2.54 mg/dl. At the most recent follow-up, approximately 3 weeks after initiation of corticosteroids, creatinine remained elevated at 3.74 mg/dl, with 24-hour urine protein of 18.8 g/d (Figure 2). This is the second report of the onset of minimal change disease occurring within a week of an initial dose of the Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine. Although definitive causality is difficult to establish, greater awareness of this potential adverse effect of vaccination is needed to determine its frequency. With prompt renal biopsy and initiation of steroid therapy, complete remission of nephrotic syndrome and acute kidney injury can be achieved. It is uncertain if and when it is safe to administer a second dose of the Pfizer vaccine in these individuals.; Sender's Comments: Based on temporal association, the causal relationship between BNT162b2 and the events glomerulonephritis minimal lesion, acute kidney injury and nephrotic syndrome cannot be excluded.  The impact of this report on the benefit/risk profile of the Pfizer product is evaluated as part of Pfizer procedures for safety evaluation, including the review and analysis of aggregate data for adverse events. Any safety concern identified as part of this review, as well as any appropriate action in response, will be promptly notified to Regulatory Authorities, Ethics Committees, and Investigators, as appropriate.

Had PEA cardiac arrest x4 secondary to bilateral massive PE with right heart strain.  Received systemic thrombolysis 9/17.  Initially in shock, likely obstcutive, and requiring pressors, though this did improve after a few days and patient came off pressors.  Also initially with metabolic/lactic acidosis, likely secondary to PEA arrest hypoperfusion.  Labs monitored with resolution.  Post arrest echo with mildly reduced EF and dilated RV.  No DVT on lower extremity Dopplers.  PE possibly provoked secondary to recent COVID-19 vaccination, though hematology felt to be unprovoked.    There was initially some concern for vaccine induced immune thrombotic thrombocytopenia secondary to patient's recent receipt of the COVID vaccine as well as thrombocytopenia.  Pf4 antibodies and serotonin release assay sent per hematology recommendation, and patient was started on argatroban for anticoagulation.  Pf4 and SRA negative with improved platelet count, so patient was transitioned to heparin infusion and remained on this throughout the course of his hospitalization.  Patient also initially with DIC, received cryoprecipitate, and labs were monitored with resolution.  He was not cooled given concerns for increased risk of bleeding secondary to DIC, thrombocytopenia, receipt of tPA.   The patient continued to require intubation and mechanical ventilation.  Initially secondary to massive PE/PEA arrest.  Continued predominantly secondary poor mental status secondary to anoxic brain injury and extremely high doses of sedating medication to control seizures.  The patient developed severely refractory seizures secondary to anoxic brain injury.  Initial EEG demonstrated status epilepticus.  He eventually required multiple antiepileptic medications as well as very deep sedation to achieve suppression. Critical Care were consulted and followed patient's course, providing recommendation.  Patient was also kept continuous EEG.  Patient was taken for MRI on 09/20 after he was sufficiently stabilized, notable for anoxic brain injury.  CT head obtained 9/27 stable, no acute abnormalities.  Ammonia level mildly elevated, not enough to explain cognitive deficit.  Per neuro recommendation, LP was not felt to be necessary given the predominantly etiology of anoxic brain injury.  Patient also developed primary lung findings of hemopneumothorax, bilateral lower lobe consolidations and pleural effusions.  Bronchoscopy performed 9/22 with removal of large amount of thick mucus, cultures negative.  Bronchoscopy again performed 9/26 with thin secretions, cultures negative.  Patient covered with Zosyn.  Chest tube placed 9/24 for hemothorax, with decrease in the amount of hemothorax confirmed on imaging.  Chest tube remained in place throughout remainder of admission. The patient was additionally found to have bilateral renal infarctions on CT as well as AKI.  Initial AKI most likely secondary to ATN in the setting of cardiac arrest.  He did not require dialysis.  Creatinine plateaued, then improved, though eventually did again worsen, unclear etiology.  Continued to make urine, though was very challenging to fully diurese, particularly given large intake from IV drips as well as hypernatremia.  Patient eventually did again develope a metabolic acidosis, likely secondary to worsened renal function.  Fluid overload caused a large amount of anasarca, particularly abdominal distension/abdominal wall edema.  Abdominal distension was initially thought to be secondary to obstruction, though imaging demonstrated no signs of obstruction and patient had bowel movements.  Patient additionally with a normocytic anemia, predominantly secondary to hemothorax.  Down trended slowly during admission.  Did require transfusion with one unit with appropriate response.  Further issues addressed during patient's hospitalization include hemoperitoneum and lower abdominal mesentery hemorrhage demonstrated on CT 9/17, improved on repeat imaging.  Chest wall fractures additionally noted on CT 9/17, though these did not require management.  The patient also had shock liver with transaminitis, though LFTs trended downward appropriately. Family was kept appraised of patient's condition and poor prognosis, particularly given severe brain injury.  Caregiving assisted, and patient's family made the decision to refrain from escalating care on 9/30.  Planned to withdraw care likely the following day once further family had had time to come and see the patient.  Patient had a worsening acidosis as well as FiO2 requirement overnight 9/30 to 10/1.  Bicarb drip was held as decision had been made for no escalation of care.  Patient expired on 10/1 at 0700.

symptom_text: myocarditis following SARS-CoV-2 vaccination; This is a literature report. This author reported similar events for five patients. This is the second of five reports.  An adult male patient (age reported as 16-20 years) received BNT162B2 (PFIZER-BIONTECH COVID-19 mRNA VACCINE), via an unspecified route of administration on an unspecified date (Batch/Lot number was not reported) as dose 2, single and via an unspecified route of administration on an unspecified date (Batch/Lot number was not reported) as dose 1, single for COVID-19 immunization. The patient's medical history and concomitant medications were not reported. The patient developed Cardiac Magnetic Resonance Imaging (CMR)-proven myocarditis shortly after vaccination on an unspecified date. The patient with no infectious prodrome developed severe chest pain and elevated troponin I within 2 days-4 days of second vaccination. The patient did not develop any other complications and was discharged home. Lag between vaccination and presentation was 3 days. The patient had fever, 3 days into hospitalization. The symptoms at presentation included pleuritic and positional chest pain; rhinorrhea; headache. The patient underwent lab tests and procedures which included ejection fraction: 53 %  (normal > 55%), electrocardiogram: sinus rhythm with diffuse ST elevation, Cardiac Magnetic Resonance Imaging (CMR): revealed patchy midmyocardial increased T2 signal with corresponding late gadolinium enhancement consistent with the acute inflammation of myocarditis. (Short-axis and 4-chamber views demonstrating increased T2 signal and LGE in the midwall and subepicardial layer throughout the left ventricle (arrowheads) in a patient who received their second SARS-CoV-2 vaccination 7 days earlier), nasopharyngeal SARS-CoV-2 PCR testing: negative and troponin I: 38.3 ng/ml. The outcome of the event was unknown.  Large clinical trials of both BNT162b2 and mRNA1273 in more than 70,000 individuals showed good safety profiles for both of the mRNA-based vaccines and no reports of myocarditis. However, myocarditis has been described after other vaccinations, such as seasonal influenza and smallpox and regulatory agencies are evaluating the risk of COVID-19 vaccine-associated myocarditis based on post-Emergency Use Authorization reports. CMR findings in the patient with suspected COVID-19 vaccine-associated myocarditis have not been well described in published reports, and the author's report tried to document some of these changes. Although the clinical presentation, CMR findings, and temporal association strongly suggest the possibility of vaccine associated myocarditis in the patient, authors cannot conclude definitively that COVID-19 vaccine was causative or that other etiologies for myocarditis can be definitively excluded in the patient. Nevertheless, clinicians should be suspicious of myocarditis in recently vaccinated patients with symptoms consistent with this diagnosis.  No follow-up attempts are possible; information about lot/batch number cannot be obtained. No further information is expected.; Sender's Comments: A contributory role of BNT162B2 to the event myocarditis cannot be fully excluded based on temporal relationship and since it is part of the product safety profile. symptom_text: GPP after COVID-19 infection and vaccination/ resulting in flare of his GPP-like eruption; This is a literature report.  A 45-year-old male with a 2-year history of HLA-B27-negative spondyloarthropathy (previously diagnosed as ankylosing spondylitis), well-controlled on biweekly 40 mg adalimumab and followed by rheumatology, presented to the dermatology clinic with a 1-week history of a new pustular rash that started on his left palm and slowly spread over his hands, arms, trunk and legs. He had a past dermatologic history of eczema and a family history of ankylosing spondylitis in his brother and father. He had no known drug allergies and was a former smoker. The patient's long-standing medication list included 100 mg vitamin C, 1000-unit vitamin D3, 20 mg omeprazole, and 550 mg rifaximin, which he took for chronic abdominal bloating concerning for irritable bowel syndrome or small intestinal bacterial overgrowth. Four weeks prior to presentation, the patient had contracted COVID-19 infection with respiratory symptoms that resolved without issue; no acute dermatologic findings were noted during the course of his COVID-19 illness. During his COVID-19 course, he self-discontinued his adalimumab given its immunosuppressive effects. Four weeks after COVID-19 infection, the patient noticed tender, painful skin lesions with moderate pruritus; he had never had such lesions before. He initially presented to his primary care provider who prescribed a 7-day course of 100 mg doxycycline twice daily for suspected infection with no improvement. Over the course of the next week, new pustular lesions appeared on his proximal arms, legs, trunk and groin. On exam, there were multiple areas of pustular lesions focally coalescing into larger plaques with involvement of the bilateral hands (left greater than right sided) and fingers. Pustular lesions were also scattered on the groin, bilateral shins, back, arms and left dorsal foot (Clinical photographs of the pustular lesions focally coalescing into larger plaques with several isolated pustules distributed on the left palm, left proximal arm, right shin and trunk, respectively. Similar lesions were seen on the right palm, groin, right shin and left dorsal foot). Microbiological data were notable for negative blood culture, and negative nucleic acid amplification tests for gonorrhoea and chlamydia. Given the desire for a broad-based skin sample and to obtain a full intact blister, a shave biopsy was performed which revealed florid subcorneal aggregates of neutrophils (A biopsy of an ill-defined yellow pustule on the left palm was taken to determine diagnosis. Haematoxylin and eosin staining (10 magnification) demonstrated a well-defined dense intraepidermal neutrophilic infiltrate consistent with subcorneal pustular dermatosis, compatible with palmoplantar pustulosis). Overall, the clinicopathologic findings were in line with a diagnosis of palmoplantar pustulosis with more diffuse involvement beyond acral sites, suggestive of a GPP-like eruption. The patient was subsequently diagnosed with psoriatic arthritis, replacing the prior diagnosis of ankylosing spondylitis. Given the suspected inflammatory nature of his rash, the patient was started on topical 0.05% clobetasol ointment daily for the first month, increased to twice-daily due to recurrent flares and new focal, painful pustular lesions and plaques on his leg and groin. One month after initiating treatment, he developed a gout and psoriatic arthritis flare and was placed on a 2-week taper of prednisone starting at 40 mg daily and restarted adalimumab 40 mg biweekly, both of which somewhat helped his pustulosis. He was also started on calcipotriene ointment and clindamycin 1% lotion, which were quickly discontinued due to lack of response. Over the course of the next year, the GPP-like rash improved, but did not resolve. New pustular lesions formed on his central scalp and upper back, prompting an increase in frequency of adalimumab from 40 mg biweekly to weekly. After 6 weeks of inadequate response on weekly adalimumab, methotrexate (MTX) 10 mg weekly was added with positive effect (Clinical photographs after several weeks of adalimumab and methotrexate combination therapy with near-complete resolution of generalized pustular psoriasis-like rash on the leg and trunk). Over the course of the following year, the patient had minimal flares. In Jan2022, he received a booster COVID-19 vaccination and self-held his adalimumab dosage, resulting in flare of his GPP-like eruption. The patient contracted COVID-19 in Jun2022 with minimal flare of his cutaneous disease and has since remained without flare.  In this patient's case, given the temporality of the COVID-19 infection with the patient's symptoms, as well as his symptom flares during COVID-19 vaccination and reinfection, a viral or post-viral inflammatory contribution to his eruption was strongly suspected. Furthermore, the cessation of his biologic medication and his underlying predisposition to autoimmune disease provided a unique substrate for disease development. We cannot know for certain the relative effects of these aetiologies on the development of his rash. However, his flares were more extreme when he discontinued adalimumab with initial COVID-19 infection and vaccination, and less severe when he continued adalimumab and was reinfected by COVID-19. Thus, we suspect that the discontinuation of adalimumab was contributory to his GPP-flares, biologically "priming" his body to develop his first psoriatic rash, which may have been precipitated by a viral immune response that triggered this autoinflammatory eruption. Cardiologist stated it was pericarditis and possible myocarditis. Prescribed 2400mg of Ibuprofen per day (which took the edge off the pain but didn't make it subside entirely, as well as pantoprazole (40mg) 2/day and Colchicine (0.6mg) 2/day. After another major adverse pain event on June 1st, I was put on a decreasing treatment of Prednisone (10mg) with 4/day for 7 days, then 3/day for 7 days, then 2/day for 7 days and finally 1/day for 7 days. My last pain event was June 15th. No inflammation was seen on the MRI with stress test July 6th 2022.

symptom_text: Day of inoculation: [I note that the nurse didn't pull before injecting] Afternoon: heavy drowsiness and tiredness, arm soreness, no redness. Evening: fever (<40C), chills, worst malaise of my life, trembling, weakness, muscle aches all over the body, exhaustion, confusion, sleep disturbance, agitation. Frecuent urination. This lasted until day 3 post inoculation. There were feelings of depression in April in the morning, with oral temperature measurements slightly below 36 C, which I had never seen before (I take my oral temperature regularly: it goes from 36.4-5, to 37.5) even after mild exercise on a rebounder. This lasted a few (at least 3) days, then the morning low temperature disappeared.  On june 1 I wrote to my therapist about my pain on my forearms. I had been trying to hang in there with it, but now it was very frequent, and I used lidocaine cream that day. I was waking up tired and on pain often, with diffuse, mild body aches, and depression. I often felt a need to stretch in the morning, for my muscles (particularly my legs) felt stiff. On july 4 I woke up with strong diffuse body aches. I wanted to rush to the doctor, but realized I couldn't drive in such pain. It was Sunday. After about 1-2 hours the pain mostly subsided. I drove to an Urgent Care. My blood pressure was 144, over what I don't remember. My usual systolic is 120-125. We talked about my PTSD, aches and feelings of depression. He prescribed cyclobenzaprine 5mg, orally, every night. I asked for my blood pressure to be taken again. Now it was 158, over 91, I think (using a manual pump this time). I take the medication that night, the next day I feel much better, and my blood pressure was back to normal. July 25 I am emotionally unstable (from being well to sadness), with chest aches, frequent dissociation (depersonalization and derealization, but never sensory flashbacks), and sudden changes in energy levels, which I blame on having been recently triggered and hormonal changes. I have increasing trouble speaking, which I also blame on anxiety, despite it being far more than usual. At some point I go to health center, where it is dismissed as psychogenic. During august I keep waking up very tired, and now speech difficulties make fluent conversation practically impossible for most of my waking time: I know what I want to say, I understand language, I can read and write, but I cannot get my muscles to respond, or to respond at reasonable speeds. This starts happening to me for a couple of days after getting triggered (which didn't use to be that way) and then the problem kept showing up even when triggers were not involved. I get a sore throat, at take a picture of it. It is just reddened. I go to Health center, and request to be referred to a speech pathologist (the person, sadly, has been unreachable ever since). September: by mid september I am still waking up with stiff muscles, sore legs, feeling tired, and by september 14 (a few days after, I notice, I had several almost non-painful sores in my throat, which then disappeared before the other symptoms showed up) I am woken up numerous times by leg movements that involve dosiflexion of one of my feet at a time (usually my left), extension of the toes, fanning of the toes, and varying degrees of flexion of the knee, sometimes to the point of raising the leg to the height of the abdomen. This may happen 10 times a night. I start to feel scared. I try cyclobenzaprine 5mg for one night. It doesn't make a difference. Almost two weeks in I decide to try to find explanations for the phenomenon. At this point, I am experiencing trembling when I genuflect or kneel at church (a daily activity for years now), I need to use my hand to help myself get up, I still have trouble speaking early in the morning and late at night, and often forget words. I have trouble bringing my laundry basket up the steps i have to: my arms won't respond enough to attempt to raise the basket, even though  I can otherwise move them normally. I end up using my fingers as hooks and going up the steps walking backwards pushing with my legs. I lose the ability to put the recliner of the pew back into place with a flick of my foot as always, even though I can put it down (I don't have a vieo of the event, I think, but I did record a video later of what that motion is supposed to be like). By october 15 I had discovered the human plantar foot reflex, and tested mine following the example of doctors in social media repeatedly. The result was dorsiflexion of the foot, with raising of the big toe, fanning of the other toes, and flexion of the knee on my left leg, no response on my right leg. I have a video about that. It kept holding true on different days, using different objects to elicit the response. I also tried other "equivalent" reflex tests, with same results. I get reffered to a neurologist. Lowering my room temperature helps reduce the frequency of the episodes. I get a referral to a neurologist. About a week later, I accidentally discover something: upon stretching my neck diagonally as far as I can and looking forward again, my teeth chatter. This stops after I push my chin on my chest. It hapens bilaterally, and it is consistently repeatable. I update my doctor about it. I am terrified.  At this point my legs are often feeling sore, particularly my thigh (frontal part). I speak to my parish priest. He gievs me the annointment of the sick. My anxiety got muh better. I start taking a multivitamin for women that doesn't contain iron, looking for a good source of B vitamins. Over the next week, gradually, I had better nights, and symptom improvement, but the Babinski was still there, the leg contractions at night were still there (just not usually wasking me up after my bedroom temperature was moved from 74 to 70F) , an with that my leg trembling has disappeared. My attempt to perform the Romberg test resulted in lack of balance becoming evident. I spoke to a friend doctor, who asked me to stand on one leg. I would stand on my right leg properly, but not on my left (lose balance). OCtober:  I have been having  tender spots all over my body. I take pictures of my touching the sponts that hurt. I also have a mouth sore in my upper lip (picture taken). Sometime I went to urgent care and was told it was probably because I was sleeping so poorly. I was prescribed antidepressants, but I dnd't take them, because I wasn't feelng depressed, and I didn't want meds that carry suicide  thought risk. I also drew and took a picture of the drwaing representing painful areas My neurologist appointment came on nove 17. She reported to not having read my history because she couldn't understand my GPs handwriting. She repeated the Romberg test, my capacity to walk with one foot in foront of the other, both resulted with me losing balance. She looked for something in my eye, but said nothing.  She tested several of my deep tendon reflexes, without any reported findings. She asked me to run my heel pver my shins: that resulted in no respnse on my right leg, but in dorsiflexion of the foot and raising of the big toe and fanning of the toes in my left foot. The same when I asked her to test for a Babinski sign. She ordered a B12 measurement, a thyroid hormone measurement, and a ferriting measurement. My ferritin level was 4.4 (4 something, that's for sure), if I remember correctly, and I was avised to talk to my GP bout iron supplementation or infusions. I started taking 65mg of iron a day since the day after the appointment. All else was great. Since that very night my legs have been awakening me again (particularly my left) with the same moveements as before. I demonstrated the chatter to a psichatric nurse yesterday )I was volunteering for something), and this time the chattering didn't stop through the usual mechanisms. I have a recording of the chatttering the day I went to the neurologist and of yesterday. This time the chattering lasted more than 5 minutes. After it didn't stop the suual way, Ithe nurse recommended that I should record it, and so I did, for more than 5 minutes. The chattering didn't end by the end of the vieo, but it did stop eventually, maybe within 10 minutes of the start. This had never happened befor I also recor mysef eating during the episode, and speaking. The phenomenon doesn't make itdifficult to eat, or swallow, and is not painful. It doesn't feel like the chattering from cold, and can happen at any temperature. I haven't been successful at trying to trigger it while lying down. I can make it stop by tensing some different muscles, but it comes back if I relax my jaw during an episode. I noticed in the video that, even whenI stop it like this, my face doesn't look quite right. I also noticed that I blinked a lot, but I don't remember if the wind was causing that. It did make it difficul for me to speak at some point, which is evidenced in the video. The mechanisms that I used and work for me when I am having difficulty speaking due to anxiety had absolutely no effect in this case. I may note that the leg movements aren't only present while I sleep, but also when I am close to falling asleep. Also, that sometimes (occassionally) they involve a rather circular motion of the foot, resulting in the foot "climbimg" up the bed, flesing upwards, thento the left, then downard as if rgoing back to the neutral position, releatedly and wuickly in a successive motion about three times or two.. Also that the contractions last a few seconds. I don't feel that I have any control over the foot during those moments. Another note, which I don't know how relevant it may be, is that I shiver very strongly:my whole back sways, my butt moves widely, my head goes out of position, and I have never seen anyone shiver like that. It hasn't always been this way, but I don't remember how long this has been. My doctor, listed here, I think, was not at the Health center when I had the severe and almost constant difficulty speaking. My academic advisor has seen it. A lot of the content of this long text has been based, not only on memory, but on writings that I directed to my therapist or friends reporting to her what was going on soon after the events took place, so when dates are stated or numbers are given they are accurate unless doubt is expressed, to  the best of my ability. I would be happy to make the videos available to you, also, if you may find them to be of help. I also had some headaches during october, but don't remember the dates. They were migraine-like, but not very intense 9except, sometimes, for a few seconds), no nausea or dizziness, or fainting, or loss of consciousness.. At some point, on a few days, I also tried using the rebounder to try to regain a bit of balance and muscle strength. I am a female, virgin, no contraceptives ever, no smoker nor do I consume any other drug, except as described, I am 5'3", 157 pounds by now (my weight has been increasing, but not suspisciously quickly). I have never had gastrointestinal issues or pain before this.  I was put on an antibiotic and pain resolved itself a few days later.  2nd shot on 31 Mar 2021  was unremarkable other than the normal fever, muscle ache, and sick feeling for 2-3 days after.  3rd shot on 10 Dec 2021 was initially unremarkable in the 2-3 day period following other than the aforementioned symptoms.  On December 27, 2021 I began to feal very sick and on 28 Dec, 2021 I tested positive for Covid 19.  Covid 19 symptoms for me included high fever, chronic painful cough, sore throat, muscle ache, fatigue, diarrhea, thick amounts of phlegm and vomiting.  I did not lose taste or smell.  I went to the ER on 29 Dec 2021 for low blood oxygen.  I was given an albuterol inhaler and discharged.  I received monoclonal antibodies on 30 Dec 2022, but they seemed to have little impact.  On 17 Dec 2021 I went to the ER for low blood oxygen at 83.  I was discharged that night with no new medication, but an Xray showed partial collapse of my right lung.    I have been under the care of a Pulmonologist since 4 Feb 2022 and am currently taking Advair Diskus 250/50 and using a nebulizer with Budesonide and Albuterol.  Remaining covid symptoms that exist are chronic cough and thick white phlegm which I cough up and have to expel nearly every minute of the day, or else I been to gag and feel like breathing is being restricted.   I am a non-smoker nor a nicotine user.  Current assumption is Reactive Airway Disease and Antibody Dependent Enhancement due to the vaccines and catching Covid 19 soon after and my Covid turning into what's being called Long Covid.   I have been out of work since catching Covid 19 and current medications are not showing any sign of improving conditions.  My Doctor  is exploring other options and has referred me to the Regulatory Authority Clinic.

symptom_text: 11/09/2021 Around noon I started experiencing flu symptoms. I was fatigued, had a low-grade fever and hurt all over. This lasted 24 hours. The next time I was sick was Dec. 1, 2021. I was sick for over 14 days with a horrific sore throat. Then I got the worse head type cold, I was up all-night coughing and had trouble breathing. I tested negative for COVID-19. I went to the ER. They did x-rays and a CT.  I was diagnosed with bronchitis, and they gave me an antibiotic and cough syrup. It started to get better the middle of December. It was at that time, my upper arm started to hurt me really bad. I thought it was because I was in bed so much and coughing so much. As time went on, my arms became worse to the point where I could not sleep at night. I can't put my eye drops in or get dressed by myself. I am having a hard time. I continue to have problems with my arms. On March 23,2022, I had an appointment with neurologist APN. I started thinking it was not fibromyalgia. I was having neck pain and upper arms still hurt. She examined and said there was a weakness in my arms. She ordered an MRI. An MRI was done on 4/15/2022. It showed interval development of modern edema in the Left C3-C4, and Right C4-C5 articulating facet and development of periarticular inflammatory stranding in the adjacent fat plains suggesting active arthropathy. Involvement of the left C4 and right C4 is suspected. There is a stable reduction at C5 and C6. There is a 5m collection of fluid in the sub tissue overly left C3. There is clinical concern for septic arthritis or possibility of a small periarticular access. Finding could be synovial cyst. There is a mild core compression and C4,C5 and C5, C6. Physiotherapy was ordered and I started it on 4/25/2022. Tomorrow, I will see a neurosurgeon. The physiotherapist, said she is very interested in what the effects of COVID-19 vaccines have on people with Fibromyalgia.

Patient states that, on evening after receiving booster dose of Moderna vaccine, she developed bloody diarrhea. These symptoms persisted for weeks. Pt. presented to emergency department on 11/22/2021 with complaints of GI discomfort, blood in stool, straining, and constipation. She was diagnosed with acute colitis and discharged from the ED with a prescription for antibiotics.  Pt presented to her outpatient provider on 11/30 with the same chief complaint. Diagnosis of colitis remained unchanged, and patient was prescribed a new 10-day course of antibiotics.  On 12/7, patient presented to the emergency department again with worsening symptoms of colitis, diarrhea, blood in stool, and GI discomfort. She was subsequently admitted for the next 24 days for major surgery with significant co-morbid complications, including:  Hypercoagulable state (new) Ischemic colitis Cerebrovascular infarction, embolic (new) New cardiomyopathy, +troponin/NSTEMI- Acute blood loss anemia PUD/gastritis/duodenitis Hypervolemia Marked hypoalbuminemia Ascites Dysphagia Severe malnutrition AKI, resolved Deconditioning  On 12/14, the patient underwent a near total colectomy with ileostomy due to new-onset ischemic colitis. Pathological analysis was conducted by providers from both Medical Center and the Health System. This reporting is below:                                                                      Diagnosis:  Terminal ileum, cecum with appendix, and colon, subtotal colectomy: Segmental active colitis with multifocal ulceration, focal pseudomembrane formation, and areas of ischemic-type mucosal injury. Associated prominent and extensive microvascular thrombosis.  See comment. Comment: Sections demonstrate contiguous involvement of the colon by a process of active colitis involving both lamina propria and crypts, areas of exudative luminal inflammation, and submucosal abscesses. While some changes of chronicity are evident, this is less than would typically be present in an inflammatory bowel disease.  The most striking feature of the process is the presence of extensive microvascular thrombosis involving both larger vessels in the submucosa and extending into small vessels in the mucosa.  In a few sections, entire vascular trees appear to be involved.  These areas are associated with ischemic-type mucosal injury.  Sections of lymph nodes also demonstrate focal microvascular thrombosis.  Because this is a very unusual colitis, the case is discussed with the attending hospitalist caring for the patient who indicates that there is an unusual clinical setting as well. Because of this, the case will be forwarded to the University for consultative opinion.  When available, this will be reported in an addendum.  Procedures/Addenda: Addendum  Date Ordered:12/22/2021 Status:Signed Out   Date Complete:12/22/2021   Date Reported:12/23/2021 15:56  Addendum Diagnosis Following examination of the glass slides at Medical Center, this case was forwarded in consultation to Laboratories, whose report reads:  "DIAGNOSIS: Colon, subtotal colectomy (12/14/2021):  Severely active chronic colitis resembling ulcerative colitis with extensive venous thrombi affecting distal colon.  Terminal ileum and proximal colon spared.  Sixteen benign lymph nodes with scattered thrombi.  See comment.  The colonic mucosa demonstrates changes resembling ulcerative colitis.  This is characterized by diffuse involvement of mainly the distal aspect of the colon by inflammation, villous elongation with crypt architectural distortion, lamina propria lymphoplasmacytosis, and crypt abscesses.  There are some areas of marked hemorrhage; otherwise usual features of ischemia, such as withered crypts, lamina propria hemorrhage, followed by fibrosis, are not present.  Moreover, ischemia typically does not have so much active inflammation.  What is unusual is the striking presence of transmural organizing venous thrombi. Ulcerative colitis does have an association with hypercoagulability and I have seen ulcerative colitis cases with thrombi, but I cannot exclude the possibility of thrombi associated with the vaccine, which also appears to have isolated reports of hypercoagulability as a complication.  Finally, we have encountered gastrointestinal thrombi as a systemic complication of COVID-19 itself. As such, the possibilities in this case include hypercoagulability related to the chronic colitis, the vaccine, or, if the patient actually had COVID-19 during this time, SARS-CoV-2.  I shared this unusual case with Dr. as well as with my other GI pathology colleagues at our daily GI pathology consensus conference.  They agree that this case has features identical to ulcerative colitis and the etiology for the findings, including the thrombi, is unclear but still may be related to the vaccine. My mind felt clear. I had my cell phone next to me, and I texted my friends and told them how I was feeling. I ran to my bathroom because I had to use the restroom. I sat there and felt like I was fighting fainting. My friends called me and I was having problems speaking. I told them I was fainting and I needed their help. They called an ambulance for me, but they are out of state, so there were problems. I contacted someone closer to me to make a call for an ambulance. I was only able to text by dictation, I couldn't type anything. My friend who I called, came over to my house right away. I had to get myself out of the restroom and make it to my front door to let her in. It was difficult. She called 9-1-1 when she got to my house. The paramedics gave me a baby aspirin right away. I felt that I could talk better after taking it. They gave me nitroglycerin as well. They put me in the ambulance and I stayed awake and alert the whole ride. They took me to The Hospital and took me right in for surgery. I was experiencing a heart attack. I had a couple of stints put in and they did it through the groin area. I was alert through this surgery. I felt sensations, but I did not feel any pain. Since I have had the surgery, I noticed that I have had some blood in my urine. I am following up with a Urologist to see what is going on. I'm very thankful for the doctors at the hospital and how they handled me.

symptom_text: With no prior known allergies or events of skin rashes, I broke out in hives a week after my Moderna booster shot. The shot went just like my other two COVID shots where my lymph node under the injected arm swelled up for 3-5 days and then went back to normal. At one week after my 3rd dose, I broke out in hives starting on my back and extending to all parts of my body (but focused in underarms, back of knees, elbows, etc). The hives did not respond to steroid injection, prednisone (60 mg/day for 4 days), or Benadryl (50 mg/4 hours, repeated for 1 week). They would appear and disappear within 20 minutes. Sometimes my hands and feet would swell to the point where I was uncomfortable wearing shoes or the gloves required at my job. I was able to get an appointment with an allergy specialist a week after the first outbreak and she said "sometimes hives just happen" and I started taking high dose Zyrtec which diminished, but not depleted, the hives. They still are present every day and are extremely itchy. Given that this is an unprecedented event, the fact that the hives often occur where my lymph nodes are located, and that peak immune response from the vaccine occurs a few weeks after administration, I still suspect that this is an immune response from the COVID booster shot.

symptom_text: I woke up the morning after my shot with the "typical" symptoms after my previous 3 shots: achy, chills, a little soreness in injection site.  Just overall felt crappy. By the next morning my pain in my gut and bladder woke me up early.  The night before I had to get up and urinate a lot (the urge to urinate, but not a lot of urine came out:  my bladder felt really irritated, but not like a true bladder infection.  It hurt to bear down to urinate, not the gripping pain at the end of voiding.  My gut was really distended, I had a lot of gas.  Burping, passing gas, and bowl movements helped alleviate the pain temporarily.  The pain was all anterior and below the umbilicus, in both the gut and the bladder, and very sharp.  No nausea, vomiting, nor diarrhea.  My stools were normal consistency, but lower in volume because I could not even look at any raw fiberous food.  My fever was 100.3.  By day 4 (yesterday), my fever was coming down and the sharpness was lessening.  My fever broke last night, and all symptoms are gone except mild discomfort in  my gut and bladder.

I started to have fever and chills about 6-7 hours after receiving the Moderna booster. I went to sleep in the evening and woke in the middle of the night with severe chills, sweating, headache, nausea, and a feeling of rigidity in the muscles of my forearms and wrists, with involuntary contraction of my hands. I wasn't in a condition to check my temperature with a thermometer. I took two aspirin, drank some cold water, and the chills improved and the muscle rigidity and hand contraction went away. I continued to have chills, headache and nausea return every 4-6 hours, into the next day, which I alleviated with 1-2 aspirin during each interval. By the next afternoon, about a day after receiving the booster, I was feeling subjectively much better and measured my temperature with an oral thermometer: it was 102 Fahrenheit. Two days subsequently, I noticed a palpable left axillary lymph node, which persisted for another 2-3 days. Altogether, these symptoms were similar but to a worse degree than what I experienced after the second dose of the Pfizer vaccine nine months earlier. However, the fever seemed higher and came on faster; the muscle rigidity/hand contraction, and axillary lymphadenopathy were new symptoms.

Cardiac MRI obtained with normal LV function (EF 64%) but late gadolinium enhancement in a subepicardial distribution within the inferolateral wall of the left ventricle at the base most compatible with myocarditis. ESR and CRP were normal. Further workup to determine etiology of myocarditis was negative (ANA, ANCA, RF, hepatitis panel, HIV, full respiratory viral panel, COVID-19 PCR). She was placed on metoprolol succinate 12.5mg XL daily and will follow up with a cardiologist as an outpatient. Family concerned that COVID-19 vaccine was the trigger/underlying etiology of her myocarditis.

MYCOPLASMA PNEUMONIA; This spontaneous report was received from other health professional via literature:  This report concerned a 66 year old female of an unspecified race and ethnicity. The objective of this study was to test a series of sputa and nasopharyngeal swabs collected in patients with upper respiratory symptoms for infection by Mycoplasma pneumonia as well as SARS-CoV2 (severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2) using in situ based methods and then to correlate the results with the clinical information. The patient's height, and weight were not reported. The patient's pre-existing medical conditions included: Patient was in good health before vaccination. The patient received covid-19 vaccine ad26.cov2.s (suspension for injection, route of admin, batch number and expiry date were not reported) dose, start therapy date were not reported, 1 total administered for covid-19 prophylaxis. The batch number was not reported. Per procedure, no follow-up will be requested for this case. Age at time of vaccination 7 decade old. No concomitant medications were reported.  On an unspecified date in early DEC-2022, patient had worsening upper respiratory symptoms with abundant mucous production including sinusitis, and an incessant cough. Patient had a low grade fever 38.2 degree Celsius and had complained of a persistent cough with no respiratory distress. The samples were each tested for SARS-CoV2 (severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2) by qRTPCR (Quantitative Reverse Transcription polymerase chain reaction) and scored as negative or positive. Patient was tested negative for SARS-CoV2 by qRTPCR. Patient had abundant mucous production with clear sputa which was retrieved and samples placed on glass slides for in situ based testing. The patient had chest X-ray and diagnosed as negative for pneumonia. A review of the cytologic features of the nasopharygeal swabs and sputa was done after hematoxylin and eosin staining. The SARS-CoV2 negative cytology showed an admixture of normal glandular cells in clusters amongst bland squamous cells with scattered mononuclear cells. In comparison, to the SARS-CoV2 positive cytology specimens which showed extensive degenerative changes in the glandular cells. The degenerative changes were evidenced as nuclear enlargement, degeneration, and cytolysis. Inflammatory cells were present, typically evidenced as mononuclear cells/macrophages with rare neutrophils and eosinophils. In comparison, the patient was ultimately diagnosed as Mycoplasma pneumonia likewise showed degenerated glandular cells. However, though mononuclear cells were evident, there were relatively more neutrophils. Further, mucous was abundant. Immunohistochemistry was next done for SARS-CoV2 spike protein (both S1 and S2 subunits) and RSV (respiratory syncytial virus) proteins blinded to the clinical and viral information. Patient was negative for both SARS-CoV2 spike protein and RSV. In situ hybridization was done for adenovirus and Mycoplasma pneumonia DNA. symptom_text: The moment the shot was put into my arm, I had a very slight prick feeling in my heart and in a lymph node under my left arm (left arm was injected).  It went away in less than a second.  Two days later, I started getting a very strong, stabbing feeling in my lymph node and into my chest on my left side.  This got worse for about 3 days, getting to the point where I could hardly exert myself.  The pain came on with exertion and tamped down when I stopped.  I also had terrible flu symptoms, including nausea.   The flu symptoms went away after 3 days, but the feeling in my chest and lymph node continued.  It has slowly gotten better.  I hardly think about it now, but I had an angiogram due to the chest pain.  I fully occluded coronary artery was found, but I had collateral vessels supplying blood around the blockage.  I am a very active person and I do consistent exercise, most often, cycling.  I still think the lymph node swells sometimes, but nothing like it had been.

symptom_text: THROMBOTIC THROMBOCYTOPENIC PURPURA; This spontaneous report was received from literature: This report concerned a 50 year old female. The objective of this study to discuss a case of thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) that developed after vaccination with Ad26.COV2.S COVID vaccine. The patient's height, and weight were not reported. The patient's concurrent conditions included: type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and bipolar disorder, and other pre-existing medical conditions included: The patient had poly-substance use disorder including cocaine use. The patient received covid-19 vaccine ad26.cov2.s (suspension for injection, unknown, batch number: unknown, expiry: unknown) dose was not reported, 1 total, start therapy date were not reported for covid-19 prophylaxis. The batch number was not reported. Per procedure, no follow-up will be requested for this case. No concomitant medications were reported.  On an unspecified date, after a week of vaccination the patient presented to the emergency department with a two-day history of shortness of breath/dyspnea. Patient denied fevers, chills, nausea, cough, sputum production, chest pain, palpitations, leg swelling or pain, bleeding, bruising, hematuria, rash, headaches, and focal weakness. She did not have any other medical conditions. Physical examination showed normal vital signs, mild-respiratory distress, and normal breath sounds, and abdominal examination was unremarkable. Clinical suspicion for infections was low as she was hemodynamically stable and a focus of infection was identified. Peripheral Blood smear test showed schistocytes. The patient's presentation and laboratory findings were consistent with hemolytic anemia. The ultrasound of bilateral lower extremities and CT chest did not show any evidence of thrombosis. The patient was suspected to have thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP). The patient's plasmic score (prediction tool for diagnosis and treatment of TTP) was 7 (high), this put the patient at considerable risk for severe ADAMTS13 (a disintegrin-like metalloprotease domain with thrombospondin type 1 motifs) deficiency (less than 15 percent activity level), prompting urgent plasmapheresis. The patient underwent treatment with corticosteroids. The patient received three cycles of plasma exchange along with a dose of rituximab. She also got high-dose steroids in the form of methyl prednisone 125 mg twice a day for five days. The patient's platelet counts slowly started to recover during that time. The patient's ADAMTS 13 level came out to be less than 10 percent with an elevated ADAMTS13 inhibitor level which suggested an acquired cause for the TTP. The patient was discharged after three days of plasma exchange; she was maintained on a steroid taper and followed up with outpatient hematology to complete a total of five rituximab infusions. The number of days of hospitalization was reported as 4 days. Laboratory data (dates unspecified) included: Plasma bilirubin total 1.8 mg/dl (normal range less than 1.2 mg/dl), Blood urea nitrogen (NR: 10 - 25) 17 mg/dL, C-reactive protein 4.9 mg/dl (normal range less than 0.5 mg/dl), Creatinine 0.8 mg/dl (normal range less than 1.03 mg/dl), Bilirubin direct (NR: 0 - 0.3) 0.4 mg/dL, Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (NR: 0 - 20) 78 mm/h, Ferritin (NR: 11 - 307) 603 ng/mL, Fibrin D dimer 9.18 ug/ml (normal range less than 0.5 ug/ml), Haptoglobin (NR: 30 - 300) 30 mg/dL, Hematocrit 20.4 (normal range 36 to 46), Hemoglobin (NR: 12 - 15) 6.5 mg/dL, Lactate dehydrogenase (NR: 100 - 220) 1126 IU/L, Platelet count 11000/ul (normal range 150000 to 450000/ul), Reticular cell count (NR: 0.5 - 1.5) 5.1 percent, and WBC count 9.4 K/ul (normal range 3.8 to 10.6 K/ul). On Day 0 of hospitalization, the platelet count was 10 K/ul, LDH 1129 IU/l, Bilirubin 1.8 mg/dl and fibrinogen was 446 mg/dl. On day 1, the platelet count was 39 K/ul, LDH 741 IU/l, Bilirubin 0.7 mg/dl and fibrinogen was 250 mg/dl. On day 2, the platelet count was 73 K/ul, LDH 401 IU/l, Bilirubin 0.4 mg/dl. This case provides an understanding of the possibility of having TTP after vaccinations, which may not necessarily be VITT. It is necessary to differentiate these two entities as the management differs significantly. symptom_text: Nausea, achy, chills, fever, headache, tiredness  All lasted approximately 24 hours

I received the shot on Friday, June 25 at about 1630 hours. At about 1500 the next day, Saturday, June 26, I felt a fever coming on. By the next morning it had dissipated, and other than a sore arm and some general fatigue, I felt better. I went to work all the next week, but on Saturday, July 3rd, I slept until almost noon, which is very unusual for me; also I awoke with a bloody nose. The only thing of note during the week was that my right calf and thigh started hurting in a couple of places, but I figured that I must have strained it slightly and that the pain would go away soon. I did take some naproxen during the week and it seemed to help.  I started doing some yard work and as I was mowing I felt like it was getting hard to breathe. I finished the front lawn, which is not very big, and sat down for about a half-hour and rested before tackling the back. Usually I do the whole thing at once and it doesn't take me very long. I found that as I mowed the rest of the lawn that I was really struggling to breathe and I couldn't take a deep breath at all. I felt like I was going to collapse but i managed to make it back inside and sit down. I must have sat for a couple of hours before laying on the couch in search of a place where I felt like I could take a breath. I didn't feel like I could pull in all the air that I wanted to, no matter how hard I tried. After about four hours I got up and went to bed, where I slept for about 12 hours and again awoke with a bloody nose. I basically spent all of Sunday, July 4 and Monday, July 5 in a recliner resting and trying to breathe. My right leg was still hurting and I still couldn't draw a complete breath.  I made myself get up and go to work on Tuesday, July 6, and made it through despite having to stop and gasp following every exertion (even walking a few feet). I took more naproxen and pushed through the rest of the week, having decided that maybe I had a touch of pneumonia and that maybe it was getting better. My right leg continued to hurt and I still couldn't take anything resembling a deep breath, no matter how much i wanted to. On Saturday, July 10, I laid down on the couch in the early afternoon and passed out for several hours. My wife, who had been out of town for most of the prior week (else I would no doubt have been to the ER sooner) got worried and checked my temperature and O2 levels and found my oxygen to be low and my temperature to be high. She insisted that we go to the emergency room. We went, and following an EKG, a CT scan, an X-ray, and an ultrasound I was diagnosed with multiple bilateral pulmonary embolisms and was admitted into the hospital on July 11, 2021. I started a course of Eliquis and as I was responding well in terms of no pain and having passed an echocardiogram, I was discharged at about 1700 on July 11. I have been on Eliquis since, and have had two follow-ups with my PCP as well as two different blood work done, both of which show improvement. I also have an appointment with the hematology clinic  on August 17. I am feeling better now, can breathe easier now, and do not have as much fatigue as my stamina returns. My right leg does not hurt any longer and the swelling is mostly gone.

After my heart rate normalized so did my blood pressure but I still felt lightheaded and dizzy and nauseated. After leaving work, I went to my doctors office. As I was being assessed by the nurse at 2:40 PM I felt another episode coming on. My heart rate was 150, I felt lightheaded and dizzy, nauseated, I felt like I was going to pass out, and I had chest pain and chest pressure. I had to lay back flat with my feet elevated so that I would not pass out. I was normotensive when the nurse checked my blood pressure. By the time the nurse got me on a 12 lead EKG, my heart rate has slowed down to 90 to 115, and appeared to be a sinus arrhythmia with increases in rate by 20 beats with any movement. For about 30 to 40 minutes I was unable to sit up because I still felt discomfort in my chest and I felt like I would pass out if I sat up. After I was able to move my heart was in a normal sinus rhythm and I was transferred to urgent care for further monitoring. In urgent care I had some blood sample sent including a CBC, BMP, D dimer, and troponin. The D dimer was normal and the troponin was negative. The BMP was normal, and the CBC was normal with the exception of A slight bump of my white blood cell count to 10.5, and a slightly elevated neutrophil count. I also received a chest x-ray which was normal. After I was discharged, I had another event at home with a heart rate of 100-115. Lead RN provided education on the different vaccines and potential side effects and client stated that made her feel better. Client denied any pertinent medical history, denied allergies to any medications/foods/environment. Client stated she had depression and she takes a weekly anti-depressant which she couldn't remember the name of,  last dose was Saturday August 17th. Client denied any other medication use. Client stated last oral intake was a pastry just before arrival to the vaccination site. Client was given a bottle of water which she sipped and a granola bar which she ate slowly. At 1040 a second set of vitals taken while seated: BP 100/56, HR: 58, RR 12, skins warm, dry and normal for ethnicity. . Client instructed to rest and relax in the chair for an additional 30 minutes for monitoring. Client stated symptoms of dizziness, weakness and lightheadedness resolved. At 1055 RN took another BP reading: BP 98/60. At 1110 client stood up and walked around the observation area stating she felt much better. At 1125 a third set of vitals taken while seated: BP 98/60, HR: 66, RR 12. At 1128 EMT took another BP reading with the automatic BP reader while client was seated: BP 96/61, HR: 68. Client stated dizziness, weakness and lightheaded feeling had resolved.  At 1145 a final set of vitals taken while seated with automatic cuff: BP 101/67, HR: 68 RR 12. Lead RN educated client on ER precautions. Client stated she felt much better and left the observation site on her own accord with a normal gait.

I received the J&J vaccine at 10:00am on March 18, 2021 at the Community Center. By about 5:00pm, I started to feel minor flu-like symptoms, but as the night progressed it got significantly worse. Around 8-9pm, I was bedridden with the worst chills/shaking I've ever experienced in my life. Around 9:30-10:00pm, I was filling water at my sink and projectile vomitted multiple times into the sink and could not make it to the bathroom. Subsequently, I ate a bagel and drank lots of water, knowing my vomitting could make me dehydrated. Throughout the night, I was awake and shaking, and drank and filled my water bottle repeatedly. At 8:00am, I was filling my water, and without my knowledge of awareness, fainted on my kitchen floor, dropping the Brita filter and likely hitting my head. My roommate heard the commotion and saw me passed out in our kitchen. He tried to wake me up and I phased in, but then subsequently phased out again 20-30 seconds later as I was trying to stand and likely hit my head again. My roommate eventually got me over to our couch and called EMTs. Upon their arrival, EMTs checked my pulse, which was fine, and saw an open laceration on the back of my head, so they took me to Hospital to access the Trauma Center. On the way, I threw up repeatedly and was very lightheaded. Upon my arrival at Hospital, I was checked for any neck bone breaks, given an IV, a CT  scan, an EKG, and staples were placed in the back of my head to heal the laceration. After my release, I was bedridden for 2-3 days and required a daily nap during work (1-2) hours for the next 1 1/2 to 2 weeks. For a while, everything was fine, but recently during the first two weeks of April, it has become apparent that my head is foggy and reacts to changes in the weather, which leads me to believe that I likely banged my head pretty good when I fainted those two times.
